topic: Command and coordination structures; ICS in NIMS

notes.front: What is the Multiagency Coordination System (MACS)?
notes.back: An overarching term for the four NIMS Command and Coordination systems: ICS, EOCs, the Multiagency Coordination Group, and the Joint Information System.
notes.explanation: MACS is not itself a structure to staff; it is the umbrella name for the four structures together.
notes.example: Like calling a set of departments 'the company', without it being a department itself.
notes.source: NIMS 2017, Glossary; IS-700.b Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 2

notes.front: What is the Incident Command Post (ICP)?
notes.back: The field location where the primary functions of incident command are performed; it may be co-located with the Incident Base.
notes.explanation: It is one of several common types of ICS facilities the IC/UC may establish.
notes.example: Like a mobile headquarters truck parked near the scene.
notes.source: NIMS 2017, Glossary; IS-700.b Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 16

notes.front: What is an Incident Base?
notes.back: A location where personnel coordinate and administer logistics functions for an incident; typically only one per incident.
notes.explanation: The ICP may be co-located with the Incident Base.
notes.example: Like a supply depot that keeps the operation running.
notes.source: NIMS 2017, Glossary; IS-700.b Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 16

notes.front: What is a Camp, as an ICS facility?
notes.back: A geographical site separate from the Incident Base, equipped and staffed to provide sleeping, food, water and sanitary services to incident personnel.
notes.explanation: Camps are satellites to the Base, placed where they best support incident operations.
notes.example: Like a satellite rest area providing food and beds closer to the front line.
notes.source: NIMS 2017, Glossary; IS-700.b Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 16

notes.front: What is an Incident Management Assistance Team (IMAT)?
notes.back: An Incident Management Team that supports on-scene personnel and/or the affected jurisdiction(s).
notes.explanation: FEMA IMATs, for example, help provide federal assistance and coordinate inter-jurisdictional response.
notes.example: Like a specialist support crew sent in to back up the local team.
notes.source: NIMS 2017, Glossary; IS-700.b Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 19

notes.front: What is Area Command?
notes.back: An organisation that oversees management of multiple incidents, or a very large or evolving situation with multiple ICS organisations.
notes.explanation: It sets priorities between incidents rather than managing tactics on any one of them.
notes.example: Like a regional office overseeing several branch offices, each running itself day to day.
notes.source: NIMS 2017, Glossary; IS-700.b Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 20

image.alt: Area Command overseeing three separate incidents, each keeping its own Incident Commander and ICS organisation, contrasted with Unified Command where several agencies jointly command a single incident.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NIMS 2017, Fig. 6, p. 44

notes.front: What is a Unified Area Command?
notes.back: An Area Command established when the incidents under it are multijurisdictional.
notes.explanation: It uses the same principles as a Unified Command, applied at the Area Command level.
notes.example: Like a regional office run jointly by several agencies, because the incidents below it cross jurisdictions.

notes.front: What is an Incident Complex?
notes.back: Two or more incidents in the same general area, assigned to a single Incident Commander or Unified Command.
notes.explanation: This is different from Area Command, which oversees separate ICS organisations rather than merging them under one command.
notes.example: Like several small fires nearby, all run by the same command team as one job.

notes.front: The four NIMS Command and Coordination structures are {{c1::the Incident Command System, Emergency Operations Centers, the Multiagency Coordination Group, and the Joint Information System}}.
notes.explanation: Together these four elements make up the Command and Coordination component of NIMS.

image.alt: Chart of the four NIMS Command and Coordination structures under the Multiagency Coordination System: the Incident Command System, Emergency Operations Centers, the Multiagency Coordination Group, and the Joint Information System.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from IS-700.b Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 2

notes.front: How did the definition of MACS change between NIMS 2008 and NIMS 2017?
notes.back: In 2008, MACS was an architecture containing EOCs and Multiagency Coordination Groups. In 2017, MACS broadened to also cover ICS and the Joint Information System.
notes.explanation: This broadened MACS to cover on-scene tactical coordination (ICS) as well as off-site coordination.

notes.front: What are the two general forms of the Incident Command function?
notes.back: A single Incident Commander, or a Unified Command.
notes.explanation: Command and General Staff support whichever form is used.

notes.front: When is a single Incident Commander designated?
notes.back: When an incident is within a single jurisdiction with no overlapping responsibility; across boundaries, organisations may still agree on a single IC.
notes.explanation: This is the default form of command unless multiple jurisdictions or agencies need joint management.

notes.front: What do Unified Command partners keep, even while working jointly?
notes.back: Their own authority, responsibility and accountability for their own personnel and resources.
notes.explanation: Together they still set joint objectives, a single ordering system, and integrated operations.

notes.front: How many Public Information Officers should be designated per incident?
notes.back: Only one, whether command is single or unified; assistants may come from other agencies.
notes.explanation: This keeps public messaging consistent even when multiple agencies are involved.
notes.source: IS-700.b Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 13, Note

notes.front: What immediate authority does the Safety Officer have?
notes.back: Authority to stop and/or prevent unsafe acts during incident operations.
notes.explanation: Ultimate safety responsibility still rests with the IC/UC and supervisors at all levels.
notes.source: IS-700.b Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 13, Note

notes.front: What do incident objectives typically focus on?
notes.back: Any two of: saving lives, reducing the immediate hazard, protecting property and environment, establishing situational control, restoring normal operations.
notes.explanation: The Operations Section plans and performs tactical activities to achieve these incident objectives, set by the IC/UC.
notes.source: IS-700.b Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 15, Note

notes.front: When is Area Command activated?
notes.back: Only if necessary, especially when several Incident Command Posts are requesting similar, scarce resources.
notes.explanation: Area Command is not automatic; it responds to complexity and span-of-control considerations.

notes.front: What is the difference between Area Command and Unified Command?
notes.back: Area Command oversees several incidents, each with its own ICS organisation; Unified Command is joint command of a single incident by multiple agencies.
notes.explanation: Learners often confuse these because both involve multiple agencies working together.
notes.contrast: Area Command spans several incidents; Unified Command spans several agencies on one incident.

notes.front: A chemical spill crosses the boundary between two counties, and both counties' fire departments respond. What form of Incident Command fits best?
notes.back: Unified Command, since the incident crosses jurisdictional boundaries with more than one agency having authority.
notes.choices:
A) Unified Command
B) A single Incident Commander from whichever department arrived first
C) Area Command
notes.choicesExplained: B is possible if both counties agree, but with two jurisdictions sharing authority, Unified Command is the usual fit; arriving first gives no authority. C is wrong: Area Command oversees multiple separate incidents, not one incident spanning two jurisdictions.
notes.explanation: Unified Command enables different jurisdictions to jointly manage a single incident through shared objectives.

notes.front: Three agencies are jointly managing a hazmat incident under Unified Command. Each agency wants to release its own press statement. What does NIMS require?
notes.back: Only one Public Information Officer should be designated per incident; the agencies' information should be coordinated through that one PIO.
notes.choices:
A) One PIO for the incident, even under Unified Command
B) One PIO per participating agency
C) No PIO is needed if the media is not present
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: multiple PIOs would risk inconsistent public messaging, which NIMS is designed to avoid. C is wrong: public information duties do not depend on media presence.
notes.explanation: Separate releases risk conflicting or confusing public messaging, so routing them through one PIO keeps the incident's message consistent.
notes.source: IS-700.b Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 13, Note

notes.front: The Safety Officer sees a crew about to enter an unstable structure. Can the Safety Officer stop them directly?
notes.back: Yes. The Safety Officer has immediate authority to stop and/or prevent unsafe acts.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, immediately
B) No, only the Incident Commander can stop them
C) No, the Safety Officer can only file a report afterward
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: ultimate responsibility rests with the IC/UC, but the Safety Officer has immediate stop authority. C is wrong: the Safety Officer's authority is to act in the moment, not only document afterward.
notes.explanation: This immediate authority is what distinguishes the Safety Officer from an advisory-only role.
notes.source: IS-700.b Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 13, Note

notes.front: A field location houses the Incident Commander and Command Staff running the tactical response. Is this the Incident Command Post or the Incident Base?
notes.back: The Incident Command Post: the field location where the primary functions of incident command are performed.
notes.explanation: The Incident Base instead is where personnel coordinate and administer logistics; the two may be co-located but serve different functions.

notes.front: Incident personnel need somewhere to sleep and eat closer to a remote fire line, separate from the main logistics site. What ICS facility fits?
notes.back: A Camp: a satellite site providing sleeping, food, water and sanitation, separate from the Incident Base.
notes.explanation: Camps exist specifically to support incident operations from a location better placed than the Base.

notes.front: A state's incident is escalating, and FEMA sends a team to help align federal activities with local priorities and support the state's Unified Command. What is this team called?
notes.back: An Incident Management Assistance Team (IMAT).
notes.explanation: FEMA IMATs deploy to help identify and provide federal assistance while operating using ICS principles.

notes.front: Three separate wildfires break out in the same region, each with its own Incident Commander, and all are competing for the same air tankers. What NIMS structure helps allocate that scarce resource across the three?
notes.back: Area Command: it oversees multiple incidents and sets priorities between them for scarce, shared resources.
notes.choices:
A) Area Command
B) A single Unified Command over all three fires
C) The Multiagency Coordination Group takes over tactical command of each fire
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: Unified Command manages one incident jointly, not several separate incidents. C is wrong: the Multiagency Coordination Group provides policy guidance, not tactical command.
notes.explanation: Area Command is particularly relevant when several ICPs are requesting the same scarce resources.

notes.front: A training slide refers to 'ICS, EOCs, the Multiagency Coordination Group, and the Joint Information System' collectively. What is this collective term?
notes.back: The Multiagency Coordination System (MACS).
notes.explanation: MACS is the overarching name for the four NIMS Command and Coordination systems, not a fifth structure.

notes.front: Two small brush fires in the same park are placed under a single Incident Commander who runs them as one job. Is this an Incident Complex or an Area Command?
notes.back: An Incident Complex: two or more incidents in the same general area assigned to a single IC or UC.
notes.explanation: This differs from Area Command, where each incident keeps its own separate ICS organisation.

notes.front: An Area Command is set up over several wildfires that span two states. Because the incidents beneath it cross jurisdictions, what does this Area Command become?
notes.back: A Unified Area Command, established when incidents under an Area Command are multijurisdictional.
notes.explanation: It uses the same principles as a Unified Command, applied at the Area Command level.

notes.front: A hazmat response focuses first on evacuating nearby residents. Which incident objective does this reflect?
notes.back: Saving lives, one of the objectives the Operations Section works to achieve.
notes.explanation: Incident objectives, set by the IC/UC, typically include saving lives, reducing the immediate hazard, protecting property and the environment, establishing situational control, and restoring normal operations.
notes.source: IS-700.b Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 15, Note

notes.front: Off-site staff from multiple agencies gather to support an on-scene response with resources and coordination. Which of the four NIMS Command and Coordination structures is this?
notes.back: An Emergency Operations Center (EOC).
notes.choices:
A) Emergency Operations Center
B) Incident Command System
C) Joint Information System
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: ICS manages the on-scene, tactical-level response, not off-site coordination. C is wrong: the Joint Information System coordinates public information, not resources and support.
notes.explanation: This distinguishes an EOC from the other three Command and Coordination structures by its off-site, multiagency role.

notes.front: A hazmat spill straddles the boundary of two neighbouring counties, and both counties' agencies agree to manage it jointly together. Which of the two forms of Incident Command are they using?
notes.back: Unified Command — several agencies with jurisdiction share command, rather than one single Incident Commander.
notes.explanation: Overlapping jurisdiction is exactly when agencies choose Unified Command over a single Incident Commander.

notes.front: A house fire occurs entirely within one town, and only the town's own fire department responds. Should this incident use a single Incident Commander or a Unified Command?
notes.back: A single Incident Commander — the incident sits within one jurisdiction, with no overlapping responsibility to share.
notes.explanation: A single IC is the default form of command unless multiple jurisdictions or agencies need to manage an incident jointly.
